You can’t put everything in a lookup table with the lookup cost being O(1).

If the things you have to memoize are super-linear, suppose you need to store some value related to all subsets of an input set of size n.

There’s no way you can do this in O(1), even assuming infinitely large memory.

I contemplated the article and it occurred to me that integer matrix multiplication is probably O(n^2), without even any galactic constants. But it will need unit-cost integer math.

First, find a sufficiently large base b so that no intermediate calculation exceeds b-1 (one pass over the matrices should do the trick). Then encode each row of the left matrix as a big value A_i = sum_k a_ik * b^k. Encode each column of the the right matrix as B_j = sum_k b_kj * b^(n-k). Compute A and B explicitly (takes O(n^2) integer operations).

Now you extract the answer one element at a time. A_i * B_j has a bunch of terms including sum_k a_ik * b_kj * b^n. All other terms have different powers of b. So do an integer division by b^(n-1), discard the remainder, then take the result mod b, and that gives (a*b)_ij, costing one integer multiplication and two divmod operations per output element. Problem solved. Can I publish in FOCS?

This is, of course, a wild cheat: even with OpenAI’s latest and greatest galactic integer multiplication algorithm, this is slower than the plain high school matrix multiplication algorithm on any real computer.

This is a misunderstanding based on mistakenly equating Manifest V3 with the blocking webRequest API. Manifest V3 is so much more than that.

Safari's original extension API, introduced in 2010, which supported blocking webRequest and indeed uBlock Origin, was deprecated way back in Safari version 12, replaced by the Safari-specific app extension and content blocker APIs. Years later, Safari introduced the web extension API, which had broad compatibility with Chrome and Firefox extensions. However, Safari web extensions never supported blocking webRequest. Nonetheless, Safari web extensions continue to support Manifest V2 to this day.

The 3 major web browsers have 3 different approaches to blocking webRequest:

1. Chrome eliminated support for blocking webRequest with Manifest V3.

2. Safari never had support for blocking webRequest with Manifest V2 or V3.

3. Firefox supports blocking webRequest with both Manifest V2 and V3. "Mozilla will maintain support for blocking WebRequest in MV3. To maximize compatibility with other browsers, we will also ship support for declarativeNetRequest." https://blog.mozilla.org/addons/2022/05/18/manifest-v3-in-fi...

Manifest V3 has a lot of restrictions on JavaScript code injection that are problematic for extension developers but not well understood by the public. Also, MV3 replaces background scripts with service workers, which is a total nightmare, but again, this is not well understood by the public.

You interact with it in whatever interface you use with GitHub PRs. It uses your comments and decisions on whether to merge PRs to guide which kinds of tasks and approaches it takes in the future.

RemainderBot runs either as a manual process on your machine or as a cronjob on a server. In tick (cronjob) mode, it checks how much subscription quota is left and how much time there is until the weekly reset before picking a task and creating a PR.

Here’s how you get started:

* Check that git, claude (or codex), and gh CLIs exist and are authenticated on your machine

  git clone https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot.git remainderbot
  cd remainderbot
  cp -n GOALS.example.md GOALS.md

  cp -n sources.example.toml sources.toml
Edit those two files with your personal goals and with sources for your task lists, respectively. Finally:

  python3 -m remainderbot snapshot
  python3 -m remainderbot run --provider claude --deadline-minutes 20 --size small
These commands will pick a task, work on it in a new branch, and will cost you a few percent of your weekly quota. Please drop a comment on what it did for you and if it got anything wrong here or in https://github.com/arimwilson/openremainderbot/discussions/6 :).

That is because if you could compute BB(n) for arbitrary n, you could run a Turing machine for BB(n)+1 steps and if it hasn't stopped yet then you know that the input corresponds to a machine that never halts. So it's impossible to compute BB(n) for arbitrary n, because doing so is equivalent to the halting problem.

Even for very small n you can create Turing machines where it's incredibly hard to prove that they halt: for n=25 you can create a Turing machine that stops only if the Goldbach conjecture is false. Though that isn't enough to prove it's not computable.

For humans, I think these are limitations because of time and scarcity, but mainly time - given sufficient time, humans can gather all of these. But individual humans do not have indefinite amounts of time. So energy, land and raw materials are scarce for individual humans, and they ascribe value to these.

For machines, I think any limitations on energy, land and raw materials would be a temporary situation, because time isn't the same for machines - a machine could simply keep doing what it's doing until it runs out of energy - which is infinite coming from the sun. Or at least until the energy budget of the population of machines exceeds the energy supplied from the sun. But that won't happen for a while. And parts that wear down are simply replaced.

On a planet as large as the Earth, again, land and raw material limitations are a non-factor until the entirety of the Earth is converted to machines, assuming the energy from the sun is sufficient to account for the conversion.
